The late Bishop Hedding used to tell an incident in his Episcopal career, strikingly illustrating the despotic power of long indulged habit. At one of the conferences where he presided a young preacher was charged with indulging too great exaggeration. Turning to his brethren in the ministry, he assured them of his determination to conquer his besetting propensity. "And regret it, said he, as much as any of you! paper from Col. Samuel Colt, of the

the first communication received from

America. The paper went over the

whole history of improvements in revolv-
ing-breech firearms. It appears that

early efforts had been made to produce
firearms capable of rapidly firing several
times without the delay of loading after
each discharge. Drawings of a number
of these were exhibited. Among old

chambers, rotating by hand; some stone

wheel locks had also eight rotating cham-
bers, and one of these, made in the

seventeenth century, had the peculiarly
igniting the charge close behind the
bullet, in the same way as that of the
Russian Needle Gun. In the United
Service Museum there was a brass mode

mechanical devices nearly similar, but

more complicated than that of Colt's
pistol. The inventor of "Nock's Patent,

in quite different manner in America

from what it is in England. In England
the greatest number of all the parts of a
gun are made by hand; in America they
are made by machinery. The advan-
tages of the latter mode are great, for the
lock of one pistol, or any one part of a

pistol, will fit the same part of another
like pistol equally well. Thus, if one
part gets broken, the fragments can be
taken out and new entire piece purcha-

offices of the injured part exactly. Only

inches in diameter; all the shots struck
the target. Scientific American.

his creed.


I believe that originally the essence of
Christianity—love to God and man, did ex-
ist naturally in the human mind, and would
have SO continued, had man not fallen.
These PRINCIPLES are the foundation of all
religious duty. Upon them, the Saviour
himself declared, "chang all the law and the
prophets." But mankind have lost the mo-
ral image of God, and these principles are
no longer the natural, ruling motives of &c.
(See Rom. I, 28; and Titus III, 8.
The whole head is sick, and the whole heart
faint."


In writing to the Ephesians, the Apostle
says, "WE were BY NATURE THE
CHILDREN of WRATH, even as others." (Eph. II, 3. Now why are we by
nature the children Of wrath, but that we
are by nature sinful? Will any thing but
moral impurity, subject us to the displeasure,
or wrath of the Most High? And if man's
nature is sinful, can it be a correct standard
of moral duty? And can the science of
Phrenology, which claims to be only an ex-
position of that nature, contain a system of
religion, consistent with Divine Revelation
as Mr. Fowler endeavors to show by this
work?


Again: The object of Christianity is to
restore the primitive nature Of man; and in
accomplishing this, it effects a radical change
in our present nature. Thus Christ declar-
ed to Nicodemus, the absolute necessity Of
such a change, saying: "ye must be born
again." For "that which is born of flesh is
flesh." St. John III. And the apostle says
They that are in the flesh cannot please
God. Because the carnal mind is em-
ity against God: for it is not subject to the Law
OF God, neither indeed can be—Roman
VII, 7, 8. "If any man be in Christ he is
a new creature. Old things have passed
away, behold all things have become new.
(2 Cor. V, 17; Rom. XII, 2. "Be We trans-
formed by the renewing of your mind"
as Ephesians IV, 22-24. "Put off concern-
ing the former conversation, the old man,
whose nature which is corrupt according to the
deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit
of your mind: And put on the new man, which
after God is created in righteousness and
true holiness" Gal. VI, 15. "In Christ
Jesus, neither circumcision availeth any
thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new crei-
ture."


If Mr. Fowler claims that Phrenology has
harmonies with the moral nature of man, as
that nature requires to be renewed be-
fore man can be acceptable in the sight of God,
How then can the religion of Phrenology
correspond with the religion of the gospel
which utterly changes the natural dispo-
sitions of the heart, Transforming the mind
and translating the soul "from the kingdom
of darkness into the kingdom of Christ" from
the dominion of sin to the dominion of rig-
eousness.


Again: Nature, as it now is, is entire-
ly too variable to be a correct standard of mo-
rals. If we follow it, it will lead one man
in one direction, and another in an oppos-
ite direction. One, in whom Destructive
vice was naturally predominant, would be led
to a career of cruelty, if not crime: while one
in whom the moral faculties were predon-
nant would abhor such a course. It is ca-
pable to see that if nature be the guide, every Gen-
tleman will be at liberty to follow his inclination
at whatever manner they may conduct. Mr.
Fowler, on page 154 of his work on her-
editary Descent, informs us that vicious
propensities are transmitted from parents
to children, and are therefore possessed ma-
terially. And If nature, as it is, be a corr-
ect standard OF duty, it follows that it is right
to indulge vicious propensities, where they nat-
urally exist.


Further; the fact that Phrenology does
not contain a system OF religion, adapted
to the present situation of man as a fallen
being, may be made manifest from his own
admission on page 186. All our duties
are connected with the atonement, which, St.
Fowler, is not included IN Phrenology. (See Rom. VIII.
For all things were created before a Savior was needed.
And Paul says: whatsoever is not of faith
is sin. Romans XIV, 23. And again: Col
ossians III, 17 "Whatsoever We do, wheth-
er in word or deed, do all in the name of"

the outset that, regarding the ocean mail service
the offspring of the wants of all of the producing
classes of the country, they have not felt at
liberty to consider the propositions which have
been presented to them in any other point of view
than as conjoined, and subsequent to the general
policy of the Government, which embraces alike every
section of the country, and cannot know nor recognize any personal local influence. This point
being settled, it will not appear strange that the
applications of individuals or companies, however
respectable, have been regarded without reference
to the personal sources whence they emanate, and
entirely with respect to their adaptation to the promotion of the general welfare.


The system of ocean steam navigation was
adopted by the Government for the joint purpose of
extending and advancing the commercial and other
great interests of the country, and at the same time,
providing marine force which might be easily
made available for the protection of American
rights, in the event of collision with foreign powers. The attainment of this double object the
motive which, in the opinion of Congress, justified the advance of public funds in aid of private
enterprise, inasmuch it was calculated to insure
to the country the acquisition of powerful means
of maritime defence, with little expense,
eventually, as the money so advanced was to be
reimbursed in money or in mail service at the option of the parties concerned, while commerce and
the arts would be promoted during the time of
peace. This reason, and this reason alone, could,
in the opinion of your committee, have sanctioned
any interference, however indirect, on the part of
the Federal Government, with an undertaking
which, under ordinary circumstances, should have been left entirely open to private enterprise.


At the time when this system was commenced,
the ocean mails along our whole southern coast
were in the hands of foreign carriers, sustained
and encouraged by the British government, under
the form of contracts to carry the British
mails; while the Cunard line between Liverpool
and Boston, via Halifax, constituted the only medium of regular steam mail communication between the United States and Europe. In this state, the commercial interests of the United States, on the one hand, entirely at the mercy of British
carriers which piled along southern coast entering our ports at pleasure, and thereby acquiring an intimate knowledge of the soundings and
other peculiarities of our harbors—knowledge
which might prove infinitely injurious to us in the
event of a war with Great Britain; and, on the
other, of foreign line of ocean mail steamers,
which, under the liberal patronage of the British
government, monopolized the steam mail postage
and freights between the two countries. Under
such state of things it became necessary to choose
whether American commerce should continue to be
thus tributary to British maritime supremacy, or
an American medium of communication should be
established through the intervention of the Federal
Government in the form of advances of pecuniary
means in aid of individual enterprise. It had been
found to be impossible for our merchants to contend successfully, single handed, against the
joint efforts of the British government and British
commercial influence. Our noble lines of packet
ships, which had far outstripped the sailing vessels
of all other nations in point of beauty and swiftness, had been superseded by the introduction of
steamers, the power and capacity of which recommended them, the best means of intercommunication by mail, and of transportation for lighter
and more profitable freights, and American interests becoming every day more and more
tributary to British ascendency on the ocean.


Under the circumstances above stated, it was
impossible for Congress to hesitate for a moment
which course to pursue, and it was determined to
adopt a policy which, while it would be in strict
accordance with the spirit of our free institutions,
should place the country in its proper attitude,
and render its commerce and postal arrangements
independent of all foreign or rival agencies.


As to the correctness of this determination, experience has furnished the most ample evidences in the
results which thus far have attended the prosecution of the system. The line between New
York and Chagres via New Orleans and its auxiliaries, have, by their superiority in point
of swiftness and accommodation, already superseded the British steamers which had previously piled along our southern maritime coast; and the United States mails for Mexico, South
America and our possessions on the Pacific are no
longer in the hands of foreign carriers, but are
transported in American steamers of the first class,
convertible, at a very small expense, into war
steamers, should occasion require, which have commanded the admiration of the world by their fleetness and the elegance of their accommodations for the travelling public. Our southern ports are, consequently, less frequented by British steamers,
commanded by officers of the British crown, whose
legitimate business it is to collect intelligence respecting the approaches to and defences of the harbors which they visit, to be made available for their own purposes in the event of the existence
of hostile relations.


A similar result has, to a certain extent, attended the establishment of the American, or Collins line, between New York and Liverpool. Previously
to the commencement of this line, the transportation of the United States mail matter, as well as
the finer and more destructible descriptions of merchandise, requiring rapidly of transmission to
and from Europe, had been monopolised by the
British Cunard line; and the British government
had, within the short space of six years, from the
postage on this route alone derived a clear income
of no less than two million two hundred and eighty
thousand eight hundred dollars, after deducting the
amount paid to the concern under the contract to
carry the mails.


Since the establishment of the Collins line, not

government and commercial interests to confine
their freights and hostages to the Cunard line,
the loss to the United States has amounted to several hundreds of thousands of dollars per annum, whilst a large proportion of the money for freights has been received
by American citizens. The effects of this increase in the loss to the United States are somewhat mitigated, because the trips of this line have been but twice a month, while those of its rival have, for a considerable portion of the time, been weekly. During
the intervals between the trips of the American
line the postages and freights must, of necessity, accrue to the advantage of the British, and consequently the evil referred to has been but partially remedied.


It may not be out of place here to remark,
that the manner in which Mr. Collins and his associates have complied with their contract speaks

stood, is not traitor to Kossuth, though he is often
represented such; formerly he was faithful servant
of his master Meulenic, then of Kossuth, and after
the 18th of August he put himself at the disposition of
the Austrians. He had no political principle whatsoever,
but admirable finances, which always provided
for the wants of Kossuth's Government and the army,
developing the wealth of the country in such way
that the paper currency of Hungary was no more de-
precated after the second evacuation of Pesth, than
the Austrian notes. He was sentenced to the gallows,
and had his sentence commuted to six years' impri-
sonment. The life of Baron Way has been very singular,
as is rich history by his uncommon and many country acts, and of no same age as
Kossuth; he seemed to be destined to much higher po-
litical station than the poor former Attorney who began his
political career with the Baron in the ranks of the op-
position in the county meetings in Szaplya. Way was el-
ected Sheriff of the county, representative to
the Diet, where he soon espoused the cause of the
Court. Though always protesting milk and water
liberalism, he promoted to the rank of Lord Lieu-
tenant and Judge of the Supreme Court, while Kossuth
was a humble reporter at the Daily. One year
later the difference of position was yet greater; Kossuth
prisoner, tried for his life on the charge of high

members of the Government, one of the officials resigned,

Way had; she had no courage to follow their example, but

able to maintain his liberal position for a long time,
and elected Keeper of the Crown by the Diet and
named Privy Councillor by the Court, and in this post-
ion he always labored to make compromises be-
tween the interests of Vienna and the rights of Hun-
gary.

a staunch supporter of Count Louis Batthyany, and was
sent by him to Transylvania as Commissioner of the
Government. But the time for compromising was past;
he was suspected by the Hungarians and denounced by
the Imperialists. He made several blunders; Transyl-
vania lost him; he was recalled by Kossuth and nearly
killed by the mob; his way corrected. But he now
espoused the cause of the Revolution with all his en-
ergies and remained faithful to the Hungarian interest
though he had before his Austrian army
in Italy. After the surrender of Villages he was also

for years without decision. In the meantime he has been

smoked upon the embers. The group
consisted of tall and stalwart warriors,
whose brawny limbs seemed well able to
triumph in any act of savage barbarity
they might be called upon to undertake.
Some of them wore frocks of buck-skin,
and leggins of bright-colored cloth, orna-
mented with strings of wampum, tin trink-
ets and glass beads, that jingled with eve-
ry motion of the wearer. Some wore fea-
thers from the eagle's wing on their heads,
as marks of rank. At the side of most of
them rested an ornamented gun, while
pouches and horns were suspended from
the branches around. Each warrior was
encircled with a belt of hide, in which
glittered the usual implements of the chase
and war. Some of the inferior ones car-
ried only a stout bow, a sheaf of feathered
arrows, and a weighty club of bone,
adorned with quills and colored feathers.

The cunning Wauchee crept cautiously
within a short distance of the camp, trust-
ing that during the drowsy hours of the
night he should be able to strike a blow;
but to his chagrin he perceived that the
party was on the alert, and that two wake-
ful sentinels constantly kept watch, while
the others slept. On the following morn-
ing the party resumed their march, still
followed by their pursuer, who hoped to
cut off some straggler during the retreat;
but no such victim fell in his way. In
the course of a day or two the roar of
waters, and the ascending mist of the ca-
teract, warned them of their approach to
the mighty Falls of Niagara; and soon
the Oneida party had encamped among
the gloomy pines and hemlocks opposite
the torrent.

On the following day the Oneidas re-
sumed their march, and at nightfall rea-
ched an American military post, then just
established at the entrance of the Niag-
ara river, on the shore of Lake Ontario
called Fort Niagara. The Oneidas en-ter-
ed within the barriers of the little stock-
ade fortress, and there established their
camp, and were soon busily engaged in
arranging a treaty with the commandant
of the place. Wauchee followed closely
after, like a blood hound on the trail, and
selected his camp in a little grove just
without the gates of the fortress.

ive speeches, which elicited frequent bursts of applause. Mr.

from the distinguished men of the country, a candidate for the

ciples, of tried patriotism, and a statesmanly vow on all great

acter, of strong convictions, and of strength in council.

olas county fully, sincerely and candidly ratify and con-
firm the proceedings of the Baltimore Convention.

ratic Convention and the Baltimore Platform, on which

victorious support.

The CALIFORNIA NEWS.—The Prometheus arrived on Saturday. With advices from San Francisco, at four o'clock of the afternoon of the 1st. We gave more news in full in yesterday's HERALD. The Crescent City arrived yesterday with the California mails which left San Francisco on the morning of the 1st. We give the specie list, &c., in another column.

The election of John Weller—originally of Ohio, late Mexican Boundary Commissioner to the United States Senate, as the successor of Col. Fremont, appeared to give very general satisfaction to the California democrats. The special message of Gov. Bigler to the Legislature, represents the State having made a very fair start for the establishment of State debt. California however, finds it, and little credit is indispensable to the development of her dormant resources. The gold lands are the property of the United States, and the gold itself is appropriated by the miners. But, independently of those, the agricultural and commercial resources of the State are still sufficient to make her, in a short time, the most prosperous and powerful commonwealth in the Union, next to New York. The mines continued their steady returns; law and order were regulating the ascendancy; there were some troubles with the numerous Indian tribes in the country; and there are likely to be more, as the poor natives are crowded back upon the mountains and deserts by the increasing swarms of the white races. In the meantime, things in California and Oregon begin to wear the cheerful aspects of established society. On the other hand, the Mormons at the Salt Lake appear to be determined on erecting a little independent Kingdom of Israel of their own in defiance of the pretensions of the general government to the sovereignty of their territory. We presume, however, that a small detachment of dragoons would bring the Saints to terms without the necessity of bombarding their City of Zion. "The saints shall inherit the EARTH" but they must not "go up to the higher law."

Upon the whole, the news by this arrival is rather dry; but business, and everything else on the Pacific coast, will brighten up with the opening of the spring.

stance, requires corresponding management,

The latter finds that the promised beauties

which were to supersede the old arrangement,

are slow in coming. The lawn of velvet, the

pride of English gardening, is merely a patch

of brown stubble; the hedge becomes topiary,

below a series of archways for the

accommodation of such animals as have no

objections to stopping.

He sees that in the race between flowers and

weeds, the latter glory in exuberance which

defies competition, while the former are behind

time, being nowhere. He discovered that

brooks, perversely, stop running in summer

when most wanted; that no skill in hydrau-

lics can make a fountain play without water, and

that the pond is admirably adapted for depos-

iting anything that should be kept dry.

self is the most verdant thing in the place, and

that for carrying out the Duke's improvements

he would be rather a convenience to have the

Duke's income. How uncertain are human

expectations! An advertisement proclaims

that a valuable and highly finished estate is

for sale, the red flag denotes the locality, and

is knocked off at the cost of the additions,

generously throwing in the original property.

A wag says it is folly to expect a girl to love

But the devotion of the people of the West
to the cause of human freedom is no less ar-
dent and sincere than may characterize
their Iowan brethren.

The virgin soil of the West was consecrated
to freedom by the architects of the Republic be-
fore the westward progress of improvement had
begun to dispute the sway of the native savages. The unimpeded advance in all the
elements of prosperity and happiness which
has marked the intervening period, has strengthened and occupied the sentiments of devotion
to free institutions, which formed prominent
traits in the character of the earliest settlers.
